source_text: Πᾶν τοίνυν, ὃ ὑπὸ ὄνομα πίπτει, γεννητόν ἐστιν, ἐάν τε βούλωνται ἐάν τε μή. εἴτ’ οὖν ὁ πατὴρ αὐτὸς ἕλκει πρὸς αὑτὸν πάντα τὸν καθαρῶς βεβιωκότα καὶ εἰς ἔννοιαν τῆς μακαρίας καὶ ἀφθάρτου φύσεως κεχωρηκότα, εἴτε τὸ ἐν ἡμῖν αὐτεξούσιον εἰς γνῶσιν ἀφικόμενον τἀγαθοῦ σκιρτᾷ τε καὶ πηδᾷ ὑπὲρ τὰ ἐσκαμμένα, ᾗ φασιν οἱ γυμνασταί, πλὴν οὐ χάριτος ἄνευ τῆς ἐξαιρέτου πτεροῦταί τε καὶ ἀνίσταται καὶ ἄνω τῶν ὑπερκειμένων αἴρεται ἡ ψυχή, πᾶν τὸ βρῖθον ἀποτιθεμένη ἀποτιθεμένη καὶ ἀποδιδοῦσα τῷ συγγενεῖ. λέγει δὲ καὶ ὁ Πλάτων ἐν τῷ Μένωνι θεόσδοτον τὴν ἀρετήν, ὡς δηλοῦσιν αἱ λέξεις αἵδε· ἐκ μὲν τοίνυν τούτου τοῦ λογισμοῦ, ὦ Μένων, θείᾳ ἡμῖν φαίνεται μοίρᾳ παραγινομένη ἡ ἀρετὴ οἷς παραγίνεται. ἆρ’ οὐ δοκεῖ σοι τὴν οὐκ εἰς πάντας ἥκουσαν γνωστικὴν ἕξιν θείαν μοῖραν ᾐνίχθαι; σαφέστερον δὲ ἐπιφέρει· εἰ δὲ νῦν ἡμεῖς ἐν παντὶ τῷ λόγῳ τούτῳ καλῶς ἐζητήσαμεν, ἀρετὴ ἂν εἴη οὔτε φύσει οὔτε διδακτόν, ἀλλὰ θείᾳ μοίρᾳ παραγιγνόμενον, οὐκ ἄνευ νοῦ, οἷς ἂν παραγίγνηται. θεόσδοτος τοίνυν ἡ σοφία, δύναμις οὖσα τοῦ πατρός, προτρέπει μὲν ἡμῶν τὸ αὐτεξούσιον, ἀποδέχεται δὲ τὴν πίστιν καὶ ἀμείβεται τὴν ἐπίστασιν τῆς ἐκλογῆς ἄκρᾳ κοινωνίᾳ. καὶ δὴ αὐτόν σοι Πλάτωνα παραστήσω ἄντικρυς ἤδη θεοῦ παισὶ πιστεύειν ἀξιοῦντα· περὶ γὰρ θεῶν ὁρατῶν τε καὶ γενητῶν ποιησάμενος τὸν λόγον ἐν τῷ Τιμαίῳ περὶ δὲ τῶν ἄλλων δαιμόνων εἰπεῖν καὶ γνῶναι τὴν γένεσιν φησὶ μεῖζον ἢ καθ’ ἡμᾶς, πειστέον δὲ τοῖς εἰρηκόσιν ἔμπροσθεν, ἐκγόνοις μὲν θεῶν οὖσιν, ὡς ἔφασαν, σαφῶς δέ πως τοὺς ἑαυτῶν προγόνους εἰδότων. ἀδύνατον οὖν θεῶν παισὶν ἀπιστεῖν, καίπερ ἄνευ εἰκότων καὶ ἀναγκαίων ἀποδείξεων λέγουσιν. οὐκ οἶμαι δύνασθαι σαφέστερον ὑπὸ Ἑλλήνων προσμαρτυρήσεσθαι τὸν σωτῆρα ἡμῶν καὶ τοὺς εἰς προφητείαν κεχρισμένους, τοὺς μὲν παῖδας θεοῦ ἀνηγορευμένους, τὸν δὲ κύριον υἱὸν ὄντα γνήσιον, ἀληθεῖς εἶναι περὶ τῶν θείων μάρτυρας· διὸ καὶ δεῖν πιστεύειν αὐτοῖς ἐνθέοις οὖσι προσέθηκε. κἂν τραγικώτερον εἴπῃ τις μὴ πιστεύειν· οὐ γάρ τί μοι Ζεὺς ἦν ὁ κηρύξας τάδε, ἀλλ’ ἴστω αὐτὸν τὸν θεὸν διὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ τὰς γραφὰς κηρύξαντα. πιστὸς δὲ ὁ τὰ οἰκεῖα καταγγέλλων, ἐπεὶ μηδεὶς φησὶν ὁ κύριος τὸν πατέρα ἔγνω, εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱὸς καὶ ᾧ ἂν ὁ υἱὸς ἀποκαλύψῃ. πιστευτέον ἄρα τούτῳ καὶ κατὰ Πλάτωνα, κἂν ἄνευ γε εἰκότων καὶ ἀναγκαίων ἀποδείξεων διά τε τῆς παλαιᾶς διά τε τῆς νέας διαθήκης κηρύσσηται καὶ λέγηται. ἐὰν γὰρ μὴ πιστεύσητε, φησὶν ὁ κύριος, ἀποθανεῖσθε ἐν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ὑμῶν· ἔμπαλιν δέ· ὁ πιστεύων ἔχει ζωὴν αἰώνιον. μακάριοι ἄρα πάντες οἱ πεποιθότες ἐπ’ αὐτῷ. πλεῖόν ἐστι τῆς πίστεως τὸ πεποιθέναι· ὅταν γὰρ ἐπίστηταί τις ὅτι ὁ υἱός ἐστι τοῦ θεοῦ ὁ διδάσκαλος ἡμῶν, πέποιθεν ἀληθῆ εἶναι τὴν διδασκαλίαν αὐτοῦ. ὡς δὲ ἡ μάθησις κατ’ Ἐμπεδοκλέα τὰς φρένας αὔξει, οὕτως ἡ εἰς τὸν κύριον πεποίθησις αὔξει τὴν πίστιν.
pass_a_gloss: Everything, therefore, which falls under a name is generated, whether they want it or not. If, then, the Father himself draws to himself everything that has lived purely and has come to a concept of the blessed and immortal nature, or if the self-controlled thing in us, coming to a knowledge of the good, leaps and jumps beyond the things that are fenced in, as the trainers say, except not without the excellent grace, the soul is feathered and rises and is lifted up above the things that are above, putting away and giving back to the relative everything that is burdensome. And Plato says in the Meno that virtue is God-given, as the words indicate: From this reasoning, then, Meno, virtue appears to us to come to those to whom it comes by a divine allotment. Does it not seem to you that the cognitive habit, which has not come to all, has been allotted a divine portion? He says more clearly: If, then, we have sought well in this whole argument, virtue would be neither by nature nor teachable, but comes by a divine allotment, not without mind, to those to whom it comes. Therefore, wisdom is God-given, being a power of the Father, it persuades our self-control, accepts faith, and rewards the knowledge of the highest choice with a perfect communion. And I will show you Plato himself, already now, considering it worthy to believe in the children of God; for, having made a argument about visible and generated gods in the Timaeus, and about other demons, he says it is greater than us to speak and know their generation, but one must believe those who have spoken before, who are offspring of the gods, as they said, clearly knowing their own ancestors. It is impossible, then, for the children of the gods not to believe, even if they speak without images and necessary proofs. I do not think it is possible for the Greeks to testify more clearly to our Savior and those anointed for prophecy, who are called children of God, and the Lord is the true Son, being true witnesses about divine things; therefore, it is necessary to believe them, being inspired by God. And if someone says more tragically not to believe: For Zeus was not a herald to me, but let God be known through the Son, who has heralded the scriptures. The one who announces his own things is faithful, since the Lord says no one knows the Father except the Son and whoever the Son reveals. Therefore, one must believe him, even according to Plato, even if without images and necessary proofs, he has heralded and spoken through both the old and the new covenant. For if you do not believe, the Lord says, you will die in your sins; on the other hand, the one who believes has eternal life. Blessed, then, are all those who have trusted in him. To have trusted is more than faith; for when someone knows that the Son is the teacher of God, he trusts that his teaching is true. Just as learning, according to Empedocles, increases the mind, so trust in the Lord increases faith.

bible_refs.note: For if you do not believe, the Lord says, you will die in your sins; on the other hand, the one who believes has eternal life.

pass_b_english: Everything that falls under a name is a created thing, whether people want it to be or not. If the Father himself draws to himself all who have lived purely and have attained an understanding of the blessed and immortal nature, or if the autonomous faculty within us—reaching knowledge of the good—leaps and springs beyond the fenced-in limits, as the trainers say, still the soul does not grow wings, rise, and soar above the things that are above unless it is borne aloft by exceptional grace. In that ascent it puts aside every burden and returns it to its kindred source.

Plato declares in the Meno that virtue is God-given, as his words show: 'From this reasoning, Meno, virtue appears to come to us by divine allotment, to those to whom it comes.' He asks, 'Does it not seem to you that the cognitive capacity which has not reached everyone has been assigned a divine portion?' He states it even more plainly: 'If we have conducted this whole inquiry well, virtue would be neither natural nor teachable, but comes by divine allotment, not without mind, to those to whom it comes.' Therefore wisdom is God-given, being a power of the Father. It persuades our free will, welcomes faith, and rewards the knowledge of our supreme choice with perfect communion.

I will now set Plato before you as one who already considered it right to believe in the children of the gods. In the Timaeus, after discussing visible and created gods, he says that speaking and knowing the generation of the other divine beings is greater than we can manage; we must believe those who spoke before, since they are offspring of the gods, as they claimed, and clearly know their own ancestors. It is impossible, then, for the children of the gods not to believe, even if they speak without analogies and necessary proofs.

I do not think the Greeks could give clearer testimony to our Savior and to those anointed for prophecy—who are called children of God, while the Lord is the genuine Son—as true witnesses of divine matters. Therefore one must believe them, since they are God-inspired. Even if someone objects more tragically, saying, 'Zeus was not the herald of these things to me,' let it be known that God himself has heralded the scriptures through the Son. The one who announces his own matters is trustworthy, because the Lord says no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (John 3:36). So we must believe him, even on Plato's terms, even though he is proclaimed through both the old and the new covenant without analogies and necessary proofs.

For the Lord says, 'If you do not believe, you will die in your sins'; on the other hand, 'the one who believes has eternal life.' Blessed, then, are all who have trusted in him. Trust is more than faith: when someone knows that the Son is the teacher from God, he trusts that his teaching is true. Just as learning, according to Empedocles, enlarges the mind, so trust in the Lord enlarges faith.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the distinction between 'faith' (πίστις) and 'trust' (πεποίθησις/πεποιθότες) and the philosophical terminology (e.g., 'autonomous faculty' for αὐτεξούσιον). Scripture citations are correctly identified and added in Pass B (John 3:36) to match the quoted content.
